runs.text: tarde, & quaſi ſol posto não ſe podia aueriguar

lines.note: Continues the preceding page: it was late, with the sun almost set, so the result could not be established. The scan supplies the lost i and the initial long s in quaſi ſol; posto retains the provisional st classification.

runs.text: a victoria, ou desbarate da batalha.

lines.note: Completes aueriguar: the issue was victory or defeat in battle. This is a continuation of the preceding entry, not a new headword.
Kessho is confiscation of all property. The divided Qex- begins a Japanese example and is roman, not part of the italic Portuguese definition; the full stop after bẽs is visible.

Qex- plus xonivǒ describes encountering this penalty of confiscation. The Portuguese reads esta juſtiça, with a final a rather than OCR esto; the compact Japanese spacing and the printed vowel mark are retained.

runs.text: em quelhe ſejão cõfiſcados, & tomados os bens

lines.note: Explains the penalty as having one’s goods confiscated and taken. The tilde abbreviations are not expanded; the visible comma before the ampersand is restored.
The confiscation includes household movable property. Hito no zaihō wo begins a second example, taking someone’s wealth as its object; qex- continues into the verb below.
Completes qexxo suru, to confiscate. The Portuguese specifies seizure by legal authority and continues with the object on the next row.
Finishes the example as taking someone’s goods, then gives qexxo no mono for confiscated property. The final Bẽs starts its Portuguese gloss.
Completes the definition of qexxo no mono: goods taken by the treasury or confiscated. Fiſco is the fiscal authority, not another Japanese expression.
Kesshutsu is explained by sugurebito, an outstanding person. The bare final t is the dictionary’s checked-syllable notation; the Portuguese first calls the person renowned.
Adds “distinguished” and illustrates the word with an outstanding scholar. The caron in gacuxǒ is visible and is not replaced with a circumflex.
The short Portuguese continuation translates the preceding example as a great learned person. It remains an independent physical row.
Keyaburu means breaking something by kicking. The principal forms and the following reference to feet make the action clear; the printed utta is retained.
Completes “break with the feet,” distinguishing kicking from breaking by hand. Pees is the printed historical spelling.

runs.text: O paßar pollo fogo, ou chamuſcar a

lines.note: This keyaki denotes singeing, literally passing something through fire. The object is the plucked bird specified on the next row, not the tree in the following homographic entry.

runs.text: galinha, ou paßaro depenado q̃ fica ainda cõ al-

lines.note: The bird has been plucked but still has some down. The scan shows q̃ fica and cõ al-, not the OCR’s q̃fica and cõ tal-; the line is an indented continuation.
Completes algũa penugem, some down; tori wo keyaki suru means singeing the bird. Vt is italic, while the Japanese example is roman.
A separate homograph names a tree called keyaki. The brief gloss does not itself provide a botanical species identification.
Kezume is a cock’s spur. The Portuguese noun is Eſporão, not OCR Eſperão; its small o is supported by the enlarged word.
Kezuru means shaving or working a surface. The scan supplies two t types in utta and an initial l in laurar, the historical spelling of working or hewing wood.
The tools and actions are an adze and planing. Ca- begins the next Japanese example, cami wo qezzuru, across the physical line break.
Cami wo kezuru here means combing the hair, as the Portuguese explicitly states. Na- begins a second example involving a name rather than hair.
Na wo kezuru means removing or erasing a name. The Portuguese dalgũ leads into the book or register mentioned below.
Completes the erasure example: removing a name from a book, list, or similar record. The historical liuro spelling is preserved.
Kezuritatetsuru is glossed as planing thoroughly or completely. The principal forms are preserved rather than converted into a modern conjugation.
Completes “plane entirely,” then begins an example about a freshly planed pillar. The final fa- belongs to faxira on the next physical row.

runs.text: xirani ixxuno muxicuino vta ari. Taif.

lines.note: The pillar bears one poem formed by worm-eaten marks. Taif. is a roman citation label; the following book number belongs to the italic apparatus. Its printed final f is retained, not silently normalized to another label.

runs.text: Lib. 12. Em hũa columna de madeira ace-

lines.note: Identifies book 12 and begins the Portuguese translation: on a wooden pillar newly planed. Ace- is the printed start of acepilhada across the row break.

runs.text: pilhada de nouo estaua hum verſo eſcrito, &

lines.note: Completes “newly planed” and says that a verse was written there. The coordinated explanation of how it was formed follows below.

runs.text: composto dos buracos da madeira como de le-

lines.note: The verse was composed of holes in the wood as though they were letters. The original st classification in composto is retained; le- continues into letras.

runs.text: tras que deixou o bicho comendoa.

lines.note: Completes letras and attributes the marks to a creature eating the wood. This closes the example immediately before the new alphabetical section.
Ki, equated with go, names the board game played with many small stones. The scan has an enlarged Q followed by capital I, not OCR M; the initial spans two physical rows.
The description continues with moving stones on a ruled board. It is transcribed literally rather than revised to match modern descriptions of go; the terminal S. is a roman written-register label.
A different ki is explained as uma, a horse. The example says that flies attach to the horse; tçu continues as tçuqu without a printed line-end hyphen.
Completes tçuqu and translates it as flies fastening themselves to the horse. The final S. again marks written usage and is roman.

runs.text: Coração, eſpiritos vitaes, ou vigor do co-

lines.note: Ki now denotes the heart, vital spirits, or inner vigor. The headword is Qi, not the OCR’s Qu; co- begins Portuguese coração.
The alternatives ki ga sanzuru and ki wo sanzuru describe relieving or dispersing pent-up feelings. Latin l introduces the alternative; the second verb continues below.
Completes sanzuru and glosses it as unburdening the heart. Deſabafar is one printed word, not OCR Deſaba far; the next example begins ki ga tsukaruru.
Completes tsukaruru, becoming exhausted; the Portuguese speaks of severe tiredness and oppression of the heart. Its final do leads into the next row.
Completes the preceding gloss and gives ki ga tsumaru with the same sense of being inwardly oppressed or constricted.

runs.text: Tornar em ſi o que eſmo-

lines.note: Ki ga tsuku is recovering one’s senses after fainting. The translation’s eſmo- continues into eſmoreceo on the following row.
Completes the fainting example, then gives ki ga tsukuru for having one’s inner strength exhausted. The printed de continues into debilitado without a visible hyphen.
Completes debilitado and explains depletion of the inner powers. Exhausto is preserved in its historical spelling and provisional st classification.

Ki ni ataru is glossed as striking or affecting the heart. The final Qi- begins the separate expression ki ni kakaru below. The narrow gap within Qiniataru is not decisive enough to overturn the aligned compact OCR spacing; that chosen spacing remains a minor caveat.

runs.text: Fazer eſcrupulo, ou tocar no co-

lines.note: Ki ni kakaru means causing concern or weighing on the mind. The Portuguese coração is divided across the column boundary and finishes at the top of column 2.
Ração completes coração across the column boundary. Hito no ki wo nadamuru means soothing someone’s feelings; the Portuguese begins con-solar. The cedilla is visible and corrects OCR racão.
Completes “console someone,” then gives ki wo yawaraguru, softening or calming the heart. A- begins the Portuguese abrandar across the row break.
Completes “soften the heart.” Ki wo nomu is here glossed as becoming deeply afflicted, rather than being forced into a modern idiomatic translation.
Completes afligirſe and adds being troubled. The isolated Qiuo starts the next Japanese expression and belongs with vxinǒ below.
Ki wo ushinō means losing consciousness, glossed as fainting; another sense begins “lose one’s” and is completed below. The caron in the verb is preserved.
Completes the loss-of-courage sense, then contrasts ki wo uru, taking heart or recovering spirit. These remain examples under the same ki entry.
A new homograph ki means tree or wood. The brief gloss distinguishes it from the preceding extended entry for vital spirit.

runs.text: Cor amarela, mas não ſe vſa ſem algũa cõ-

lines.note: Another ki means yellow; the dictionary says this form is used in a compound. The abbreviated cõ- continues into composição below.
Completes composição, with the i omitted by OCR now restored. Ki iro ni naru means becoming yellow; its Portuguese amarelo is divided across rows.
Completes “become yellow” and gives qina iro for the yellow color. The scan separates Qina from iro; this is not a reason to regularize the historical adjectival form.
Kiru means putting on clothing; yoroi wo kiru applies it to wearing armor. The printed principal forms are retained.
The armor example means arming oneself. A metaphorical use, on wo kiru, means receiving a favor or benefit; Per met. belongs to the italic apparatus.
Completes receber beneficios, the translation of on wo kiru. The short line is a genuine continuation rather than a separate entry.
A different verb, kuru, means coming. Kochi e koi is the imperative “come here,” matched by Vẽ cà; the Portuguese abbreviation and grave accent are retained.
Kyakka is explained as ashi no shita, beneath the feet. The scan has two e types in pees, not the OCR’s pes.

Kyak kon is explained with hagi and kubisu and glossed as heel or feet. The second pass confirms the printed comma after Qiaccon. The roman cubiſu has long s, not f; the historical alternatives are retained without harmonizing their anatomical scope.

Kyaku, equated with marebito, means a guest. The far-right parenthesis and hoſpedes. are a displaced continuation of the next line’s lodging-house definition, not an extra gloss of this headword; their printed position is preserved.

runs.text: Hoſpedaria, ou caſaõde ſe agaſalhã os

lines.note: Kyakuden is a lodging or house where guests are accommodated. Its final hoſpedes. was set at the far right of the preceding physical row. The entire headword is roman; OCR’s isolated italic ẽ and the false break in agaſalhã are removed.
Kyakujin is another term for guest, again explained by marebito. The Japanese synonym is not a word embedded inside a Portuguese explanatory sentence.
Kyakurai is unpacked as marebito kitaru, a guest coming, although the Portuguese simply says “guest.” The scan clearly has Qia-, not OCR Qua-.
Kyakuro is explained as tsukabashira: short supporting posts. The scan has Qia-, not Qua-; the abbreviated colũ- continues into columnas.

runs.text: nas curtas que aßentaõ ſobre outros paos, ou tra

lines.note: Describes short posts resting on other timbers or beams. Tra continues into traues without a printed hyphen at this row’s right edge.

runs.text: ues pera ſobre ellas aßentarem outros paos.

lines.note: Completes traues and explains that more timbers rest on these short posts. This is the load-bearing arrangement described by the definition, not a new example.
Kyakusō is a visiting or itinerant religious person. The scan’s vowel mark is a circumflex, not OCR caron, and the Portuguese reads hoſpede rather than boſpede.
Kyakusei is directly glossed as a comet. The transcription does not substitute a modern astronomical category for the dictionary’s stated meaning.
Kyakushin is explained as hedataru kokoro, a detached or distant heart. There is no secure printed full stop after the headword, so none is supplied.
The Portuguese describes a somewhat distant, not very familiar disposition. Qia- begins the example below; the OCR’s spurious internal space is removed.
Completes kyakushin ni zonzuru, feeling some distance or estrangement. The Portuguese alienação here concerns reserve toward others, not a diagnosis.
Completes the inward-estrangement gloss, then gives kyakushingamashii ii yō, a distant way of speaking. The final Ma continues into maneira without a visible hyphen.

runs.text: neira de falar algum tanto alienado, & diffe-

lines.note: Completes maneira and describes speech showing some distance or difference in feeling. Diffe- continues into differente.
Completes differente no animo, keeping the explanation tied to the speaker’s disposition. The short continuation is retained as a separate physical row.

runs.text: Hũas como meas calças que tomão dos

lines.note: Kyahan are traveling leggings, described as partial hose extending from the knees. The visible headword is Qiafan, not OCR Quafan; the definition continues below.

runs.text: joelhos tè perto do artelho pera caminhar.

lines.note: The leggings extend from the knees to near the ankle and are used for walking. The Portuguese spelling and the grave in tè are retained.

runs.text: Pano branco interior que cingẽ as mo-

lines.note: Kyafu names a white undercloth worn by women below the waist. The visible letter is f, not long s. After independent scan reading, the supplied NINJAL index also confirms Qiafu (Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0).
Completes molheres and locates the garment from the waist downward. The historical spelling molheres is not modernized.
Kyamojina, alternatively kyasha, describes something refined, neat, or clean. The printed alternative marker l has no clearly visible following comma here, unlike many neighboring entries.
Adds a pleasing appearance and explicitly labels the expression as women’s speech. This usage note qualifies the preceding Japanese alternatives.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de auental que cingem

lines.note: Kyappu is described as a kind of apron tied around the body. The wearers are identified on the next row; auental retains the historical u/v spelling.
Specifies that Buddhist clergy wear this apron over their clothing. Bonzos is the Portuguese wording of the gloss, not a Japanese term to mark for font toggling.
Kyara is glossed by Calambà, the fragrant aloeswood term. The printed grave accent is preserved; the gloss is not expanded into a botanical classification.
Kyatat and kyatatsu, explained by ashitsugi, name a raised working platform. The first form preserves final checked t; the row starts at the normal headword margin, not the OCR’s continuation indent.

runs.text: alto de quatro pees de que vſão nas obras pe

lines.note: The platform is a high four-footed stand used in building work. Pees has two e types; the terminal pe continues into pera without an added hyphen.
Completes pera and explains the purpose: reaching high places. This closes the platform definition.
Kyatatsu is cross-referred to the preferred form kyatat. The italic Latin word is Meliùs, not OCR Meltis; the small grave over u is retained after enlargement.
Kiatsumaru means coming together or assembling. It is ki plus atsumaru, not the ky- contraction suggested by the initial kana hint; the scan has Q, not OCR G.
Shohō yori kiatsumaru means assembling from all directions. The first o of Xofǒ is crossed by a stain, but the surviving types support the reading; the final long vowel retains its caron.
Completes todas as partes, from all sides. The scan does not establish the OCR’s grave accent on as; the nearby diagonal stain is not transcribed as an accent.
